title_en: Cheng Junping v. Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over confirmation of shareholder qualification
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over confirmation of shareholder qualification; First instance; Basic People's Court; Shanghai Municipality; Natural person; Legal person; Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China; Conditions for disclosure of foreign anonymous shareholders; Application of negative list for foreign investment; Confirmation of shareholder qualification; Supporting the plaintiff; Anonymous investment; Shareholding by proxy; Foreign investment access; Dispute over confirmation of shareholder qualification in a limited liability company, etc.
full_text_en:
Carson Jun Ping Cheng v. Shanghai New Star Import & Export Co., Ltd. et al.

— Dispute over confirmation of shareholder qualification

[Case Summary]

The Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China adopts a pre-entry national treatment and negative list management model for foreign investment. Where an undisclosed foreign shareholder petitions for confirmation of shareholding and registration as a disclosed shareholder, if the undisclosed shareholder has proven that he or she has actually made an investment and possesses a recognized shareholder status, and if the field in which the company engages does not fall within the scope of the negative list for foreign investment, the people's court may confirm his or her change to a disclosed shareholder; if the field in which the company engages falls within a restricted category on the negative list, the consent of the competent foreign investment authority must also be obtained.

Plaintiff: Carson Jun Ping Cheng, male, born on September 25, 1962, a national of the United States of America, residing in Pudong New Area, Shanghai.

Defendant: Shanghai New Star Import & Export Co., Ltd., domiciled at Jinyu Road, China (Shanghai) Pilot Free Trade Zone.

Legal Representative: Zhang Feng, Executive Director of the company.

Third Party: Zhang Feng, male, born on January 19, 1970, Han nationality, residing in Jinan, Shandong Province.

Third Party: Cheng Lan, male, born on October 2, 1979, Han nationality, residing in Jingzhou, Hubei Province.

The plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, filed an action with the Pudong New Area People's Court of Shanghai against the defendant, Shanghai New Star Import & Export Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "New Star Company"), and the third parties, Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan, concerning a dispute over confirmation of shareholder qualification.

Plaintiff's Allegations: In November 2009, Cheng, Zhang Feng, and Cheng Lan reached a consensus to establish a new trading company in Shanghai to provide import and export services for Ncstar Company, which Cheng had established in the United States, with a registered capital of RMB (all currencies below are in RMB unless otherwise specified) 1,000,000. On November 3, 2009, capital contributions of RMB 510,000 and RMB 490,000 were actually paid in the names of Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan, respectively, to the defendant New Star Company. On the date of capital verification, Cheng entrusted Cheng Lan to pay Zhang Feng RMB 458,762, of which RMB 260,000 was Cheng's capital contribution. On November 10, 2009, the three parties signed a "Share Agreement" in Pudong New Area, Shanghai, confirming that Cheng contributed RMB 510,000, and Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan contributed RMB 250,000 and RMB 240,000, respectively. Given that Cheng is a U.S. national and could not establish a joint venture with domestic individuals, the three parties decided to initially establish the company in the names of Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan, with Zhang Feng serving as the legal representative of New Star Company. On September 10, 2012, New Star Company acquired 100% of the equity of Shanghai Yiyue Investment Management Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Yiyue Company") by way of equity transfer. To clarify the proportion of investment equity and rights and interests, on October 29, 2012, the parties signed another "Share Agreement," which again specified the equity proportions of the three parties in New Star Company. Before and after the signing of the "Share Agreement" on November 10, 2009, Cheng had been continuously involved in the daily operations and management of New Star Company, participated in decision-making, exercised shareholders' rights, reviewed and approved reports of the executive director, and made corresponding decisions. Cheng repeatedly requested Zhang Feng to transfer the 26% equity of New Star Company held by Zhang Feng on behalf of Cheng to Cheng Lan, but Zhang Feng refused and claimed to be the actual owner of 51% of the equity of New Star Company. Therefore, Cheng filed this lawsuit, requesting the court to: 1. Confirm that the 26% equity of New Star Company registered under Zhang Feng's name belongs to Cheng; 2. Order New Star Company to cooperate with Cheng in registering the transfer of the 26% equity held by Zhang Feng to Cheng's name.

Defendant's Defense: 1. The plaintiff, Cheng, did not contribute capital or subscribe for contributions to New Star Company. The so-called capital contribution by Cheng was due to multiple creditor-debt relationships between the third parties Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan at the time. Cheng is Cheng Lan's elder brother. Before Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan's relationship broke down, Cheng Lan had kept blank signed pages bearing the official seal of New Star Company, and Cheng Lan used the blank signed pages to forge a "Capital Contribution Certificate." The seal on the "Capital Contribution Certificate" was affixed much earlier than the text of the certificate was typed. 2. The "Share Agreement" signed on November 10, 2009, was not actually performed. After Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan cooperated to establish New Star Company, Cheng proposed to deepen the cooperative relationship with Zhang Feng by establishing a Sino-foreign joint venture between himself and New Star Company, promising to contribute 51% of the capital and requiring New Star Company to move all its business into the Sino-foreign joint venture for operation in the future. For this purpose, Cheng, Zhang Feng, and Cheng Lan signed the "Share Agreement." However, after the "Share Agreement" was signed, the parties failed to finalize the specific details, and the Sino-foreign joint venture was never actually established. Cheng also did not contribute 51% of the capital to New Star Company after signing the "Share Agreement." 3. The "Share Agreement" signed on October 29, 2012, was a guarantee for a loan to New Star Company, not a genuine investment relationship. After New Star Company was established, Cheng Lan lent money to New Star Company on nine occasions, totaling RMB 10,310,000, of which a large portion came from Cheng. New Star Company repaid the loan on 21 occasions, fully repaying all amounts. To acquire the equity of Yiyue Company, on September 7, 2012, Cheng Lan lent New Star Company a lump sum of RMB 2,450,000. To ensure the safety of Cheng's funds, Cheng required Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan to sign the "Share Agreement," but never requested any actual registration of equity transfer. 4. Even if Cheng's capital contribution was established, it violated a mandatory provision of law and should be null and void. Cheng, as a foreign national, established a Sino-foreign equity joint venture with Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan, which violated Article 1 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Sino-Foreign Equity Joint Ventures and was therefore invalid.

Statements of Third Party Zhang Feng: Consistent with the defense of the defendant New Star Company.

Statements of Third Party Cheng Lan: Consistent with the allegations of the plaintiff Cheng.

Facts Found by the Pudong New Area People's Court of Shanghai at First Instance

On November 10, 2009, the plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, and the third parties, Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan, signed a "Share Agreement" stipulating that, after consultation among the three parties, they agreed to establish a trading company in Shanghai. Since Cheng is a U.S. national and could not at that time establish a joint venture with domestic individuals, after discussion, the three parties agreed to initially establish the company in the names of Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan. When conditions were ripe, Cheng would establish a Sino-foreign joint venture with the company, and the capital contributions of each party would still be made according to the agreed proportions. The three parties now reached the following agreement: 1. The three parties agreed to establish the defendant New Star Company in the names of Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan; 2. Although New Star Company was established in the names of Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan, the actual investment proportions were: Cheng 51%, Zhang Feng 25%, and Cheng Lan 24%. Zhang Feng was to serve as the legal representative. The registered capital was RMB 1,000,000, with Cheng contributing RMB 510,000, Zhang Feng contributing RMB 250,000, and Cheng Lan contributing RMB 240,000. Cheng held 51% of the equity of the company.

On November 3, 2009, the plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, transferred RMB 458,762 to the third party, Zhang Feng, through the third party, Cheng Lan. Cheng and Cheng Lan both stated that among the RMB 458,762, RMB 260,000 was Cheng's capital contribution to the defendant New Star Company made in the name of Zhang Feng, and another RMB 250,000 of Cheng's contribution was included in Cheng Lan's RMB 490,000 contribution.

On November 5, 2009, Shanghai Huiqiang Accounting Firm issued a "Capital Verification Report" stating that the registered capital applied for by the defendant New Star Company (in preparation) was RMB 1,000,000, and the initial capital contributions of all shareholders had been fully paid. Upon verification, as of November 3, 2009, New Star Company (in preparation) had received total registered capital contributions of RMB 1,000,000 from all shareholders, all paid in monetary form according to the proportions stipulated in the company's articles of association. The appendix to the "Capital Verification Report," the "Detailed List of Paid-in Registered Capital for This Period," stated that Zhang Feng contributed RMB 510,000, accounting for 51% of the registered capital, and Cheng Lan contributed RMB 490,000, accounting for 49% of the registered capital. The appendix "Bank Statement" showed that on November 3, 2009, Zhang Feng transferred RMB 510,000 to the New Star Company account, and Cheng Lan transferred RMB 490,000 to the New Star Company account.

On November 11, 2009, the defendant New Star Company was established as a limited liability company (invested or controlled by natural persons), with the legal representative being the third party, Zhang Feng, registered capital of RMB 1,000,000, and shareholders being Zhang Feng (holding 51% equity) and the third party, Cheng Lan (holding 49% equity).

On October 29, 2012, the plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, and the third parties, Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan, signed another "Share Agreement" stipulating that in September 2012, after consultation among Cheng, Zhang Feng, and Cheng Lan, the shareholders' resolution was as follows: the defendant New Star Company would acquire 100% of the equity of Yiyue Company by way of equity acquisition. New Star Company would hold 100% of the equity of Yiyue Company. According to the respective shareholding proportions of the three parties in New Star Company, the actual ownership proportions of the three parties in Yiyue Company were as follows: Cheng held 51% of the company's equity, Zhang Feng held 25% of the company's equity, and Cheng Lan held 24% of the company's equity.

On August 6, 2018, the defendant New Star Company issued a "Capital Contribution Certificate" to the plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, stating that Cheng had paid a capital contribution of RMB 510,000 to New Star Company on November 3, 2009. During the litigation, New Star Company and the third party, Zhang Feng, objected to this "Capital Contribution Certificate," claiming that it had been subsequently printed by the third party, Cheng Lan, on a blank signed page bearing the official seal of New Star Company without authorization. To this end, both parties jointly commissioned the Institute of Forensic Science of the Ministry of Justice to conduct a forensic examination on "the time of formation of the New Star Company seal impression on the 'Capital Contribution Certificate,' the time of formation of the printed text, and the chronological order of the formation of the New Star Company seal impression and the printed text." The Institute of Forensic Science issued a "Forensic Opinion," which concluded as follows: (1) The "New Star Company" seal impression on the examined "Capital Contribution Certificate" was not affixed between December 31, 2009, and April 20, 2012, but it is impossible to determine whether it was affixed on the issuance date of "August 6, 2018"; (2) It is impossible to determine the time of formation of the printed text on the examined "Capital Contribution Certificate"; (3) It is impossible to determine the chronological order of the formation of the "New Star Company" seal impression and the printed text on the examined "Capital Contribution Certificate."

It was also established that between 2009 and 2018, the third party, Zhang Feng, had numerous email exchanges with the plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, and the third party, Cheng Lan, via email addresses such as zhangfeng0117@gmail.com, zhangfeng_117@126.com, and frank_f1@163.com, reporting on the operations of the defendant New Star Company and related enterprises. Among them, on January 7, 2010, Cheng Lan sent an email titled "Office Accounts" to Zhang Feng's email address zhangfeng_117@126.com. The attachment to the email, "Capital Contributions of Shareholders of New Star Company," stated: Cheng accounted for 51%, with a capital contribution of RMB 510,000; Zhang Feng accounted for 25%, with a capital contribution of RMB 250,000 (registered amount RMB 510,000, of which 26% (RMB 260,000) was Cheng's shares); Cheng Lan accounted for 24%, with a capital contribution of RMB 240,000 (registered amount RMB 490,000, of which 25% (RMB 250,000) was Cheng's shares). On September 16, 2013, Zhang Feng sent an email from zhangfeng_117@126.com to Cheng stating: "Dear Carson, Please see the attachment. As you requested, I have written the following proposal. Please review. Thank you!" The attachment to this email, "Dividend Plan of New Star Company," stated that as of December 31, 2011, total profits of New Star Company amounted to RMB 11,391,327. By resolution of the shareholders, RMB 10,000,000 of this amount was to be distributed as dividends to the shareholders. The distribution according to the shareholding proportions of each shareholder was as follows: Cheng RMB 5,100,000; Zhang Feng RMB 2,500,000; Cheng Lan RMB 2,400,000. By unanimous agreement of the shareholders, the following amounts were paid to each shareholder in proportion: Cheng RMB 4,249,999; Zhang Feng RMB 2,500,000; Cheng Lan RMB 2,200,000. The remaining unpaid dividend amount was to be reinvested in the company as capital contributions of each shareholder. Additionally, the undistributed profits of RMB 1,391,327 were to remain in the company as working capital.

Opinion of the Court (First Instance of Pudong New Area People's Court of Shanghai):

This case is a dispute over confirmation of shareholder qualification. Since the plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, is a U.S. national, this case involves a foreign element. Article 14 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations stipulates that matters such as the civil capacity, civil conduct capacity, organizational structure, and shareholders' rights and obligations of a legal person and its branches shall be governed by the law of the place of registration. The registered place of the subject company, the defendant New Star Company, is located in the People's Republic of China. Therefore, the laws of the People's Republic of China shall apply to the trial of this case.

The issues in dispute in this case are as follows:

1. Whether the third party, Zhang Feng, held on behalf of the plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, 26% of the equity of the defendant New Star Company.

2. Whether Cheng can request New Star Company to handle the corresponding equity transfer procedures, and whether there are legal or policy obstacles to such a change.

Regarding Issue 1:

First, there is a series of clear agreements mutually corroborating that the plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, actually holds 51% of the equity of the defendant New Star Company. The "Share Agreement" signed on November 10, 2009, the "Share Agreement" signed on October 29, 2012, and the "Capital Contribution Certificate" issued on August 6, 2018, all represent the true intentions of the parties and confirm that Cheng actually holds 51% of the equity of New Star Company, of which 26% is held on his behalf by the third party Zhang Feng, and 25% is held on his behalf by the third party Cheng Lan. Second, Cheng has provided evidence to prove that he fulfilled the corresponding capital contribution obligations to New Star Company. Cheng claims that among the RMB 458,762 transferred by Cheng Lan to Zhang Feng on November 3, 2009, RMB 260,000 was Cheng's contribution made in the name of Zhang Feng. Cheng Lan acknowledges this and also admits that RMB 250,000 of his own RMB 490,000 contribution was actually contributed by Cheng. Although New Star Company and Zhang Feng deny this, they have not provided sufficient evidence to support their denial. Moreover, based on the subsequent "Share Agreement," "Capital Contribution Certificate," and dividend plan, it can be inferred that Cheng has actually fulfilled his capital contribution obligations. Finally, a series of email exchanges among the parties shows that Cheng actually participated in the management and operation of New Star Company, particularly in major decision-making, and exercised his rights and obligations as a major shareholder. As for Zhang Feng's defense that the "Capital Contribution Certificate" was subsequently forged by Cheng Lan, the court of first instance holds that, on the one hand, the "Forensic Opinion" did not reach a definitive conclusion, and Cheng did not provide other evidence to corroborate it; on the other hand, all parties acknowledge that the official seal on the "Capital Contribution Certificate" is genuine. Even if Cheng Lan printed the "Capital Contribution Certificate" on a blank signed page, this is an internal management issue of New Star Company and does not affect the court's determination of the actual owner of the equity of New Star Company based on a comprehensive review of all evidence. Accordingly, the court of first instance finds that Cheng is the undisclosed shareholder of New Star Company, and the actual owner of the 26% equity of New Star Company registered under Zhang Feng's name is Cheng.

Regarding Issue 2:

The defendant New Star Company is a limited liability company (invested or controlled by natural persons). The disclosed shareholders are the third parties Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan, both domestic individuals. The undisclosed shareholder is the plaintiff, Carson Jun Ping Cheng, a U.S. national. The main disputes concerning the change of the corresponding industrial and commercial registration to disclose the undisclosed shareholder are as follows:

1. Whether domestic individuals can establish a foreign-invested enterprise with a foreign national. Article 1 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Sino-Foreign Equity Joint Ventures allowed foreign companies, enterprises, other economic organizations, or individuals to establish joint ventures with Chinese companies, enterprises, or other economic organizations. Although this law did not include Chinese individuals as domestic joint venture partners, it was repealed on January 1, 2020. The subsequently effective Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China does not impose such restrictions. Article 2 of that law clearly stipulates that foreign-invested enterprises refer to enterprises wholly or partially invested by foreign investors, registered and established in China in accordance with Chinese law. Article 3 of the Regulations for the Implementation of the Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China further clarifies that "other investors" in Article 2 of the Foreign Investment Law include Chinese individuals. Meanwhile, according to Article 2 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China: "Where an investment contract relates to areas outside the negative list for foreign investment access, if a party claims that the contract is invalid or not yet effective on the grounds that it has not been approved or registered by the competent administrative department, the people's court shall not support such claim. If an investment contract as provided in the preceding paragraph was concluded before the implementation of the Foreign Investment Law, but the people's court has not yet rendered a final judgment at the time of the implementation of the Foreign Investment Law, the validity of the contract shall be determined by applying the provisions of the preceding paragraph." Therefore, in this case, the court of first instance does not support the request of the defendant New Star Company and the third party Zhang Feng to confirm that the act of the plaintiff Cheng establishing a company with the third parties Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan is invalid.

2. Whether a foreign national becoming a shareholder of a company requires undergoing relevant approval procedures. After the Foreign Investment Law took effect, China implemented a pre-entry national treatment plus negative list management system for foreign investment. Pre-entry national treatment refers to the treatment granted to foreign investors and their investments in the investment access stage that is no less favorable than that granted to domestic investors and their investments. A negative list refers to special access management measures implemented by the state for foreign investment in specific areas. The state grants national treatment to foreign investment outside the negative list. In this case, the court of first instance specifically sent a letter to the Shanghai Municipal Commission of Commerce to inquire as to "whether, if Cheng is confirmed as a shareholder of the defendant, the Shanghai Municipal Commission of Commerce agrees to change Cheng to a shareholder of the defendant and change the defendant to a foreign-invested enterprise." The Investment Promotion Division of the Pudong New Area Commerce Commission of Shanghai replied in a letter: "...The field in which New Star Company engages does not fall within the scope of the Special Access Management Measures for Foreign Investment (Negative List). There is no legal obstacle for our commission to handle the filing procedures for the change of Carson Jun Ping Cheng to a shareholder of New Star Company and the change of New Star Company to a foreign-invested enterprise." Therefore, the plaintiff Cheng's request to become a shareholder of the defendant New Star Company does not require special approval procedures, nor are there legal obstacles.

3. Regarding the internal corporate procedures for shareholder changes. According to Article 24 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China (III), where an actual investor requests the company to change the shareholder, issue a capital contribution certificate, record the investor in the register of shareholders and the company's articles of association, and register with the company registration authority, the consent of more than half of the other shareholders of the company is required. In this case, all other shareholders except the third party Zhang Feng, namely the third party Cheng Lan, expressly recognized the plaintiff Cheng Junping's status as a shareholder and also agreed to register Cheng Junping as a shareholder of the defendant Niuxinda Company. Therefore, Cheng Junping's request that Niuxinda Company register the 26% equity held by Zhang Feng on his behalf in Cheng Junping's name complies with the provisions of the law and judicial interpretations, and the first-instance court supported it in accordance with the law.

In summary, the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court, pursuant to Article 14 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, Articles 2 and 4 of the Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 3 of the Implementing Regulations of the Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 22 and 24 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China (III), Article 2 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 90 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on January 2, 2020:

I. It is confirmed that the 26% equity of the defendant Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Co., Ltd. registered in the name of the third party Zhang Feng is owned by the plaintiff Cheng Junping (Carson Jun Ping Cheng);

II. The defendant Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Co., Ltd. shall, within fifteen days from the effective date of the judgment, register the 26% equity of Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Co., Ltd. held in the name of the third party Zhang Feng to the name of the plaintiff Cheng Junping (Carson Jun Ping Cheng), and Zhang Feng shall cooperate.

Niuxinda Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court.

Niuxinda Company appealed, arguing that: 1. The first-instance judgment erroneously determined the expression of intent in the two Share Agreements. The Share Agreement signed in 2009 meant that a joint venture would be established in the future between Niuxinda Company and the appellee Cheng Junping, rather than the establishment of Niuxinda Company itself. The Share Agreement signed in 2012 was a guarantee for Niuxinda Company's loan to purchase shares of Yiyue Company. 2. The first-instance court erroneously accepted the appraisal conclusion of the Capital Contribution Certificate. The appraisal conclusion could not determine that the Capital Contribution Certificate was stamped on August 6, 2018. In light of multiple sample materials, particularly the sample materials submitted by Cheng Junping in another case with the same date, the samples and the examined materials were contradictory. 3. The first-instance court erroneously determined that the two email addresses zhangfeng0117@gmail.com and zhangfeng_117@126.com belonged to the third party at first instance, Zhang Feng. The first-instance court merely relied on Cheng Junping's unilateral assertion to establish this fact, which could not be corroborated by other evidence. Niuxinda Company requested that the second-instance court set aside the first-instance judgment and remand the case for retrial or amend the judgment to dismiss all of Cheng Junping's first-instance claims.

The appellee Cheng Junping responded, arguing that: 1. The content of the two Share Agreements contradicted the appellant Niuxinda Company's statements; on the contrary, the agreements stated that Cheng Junping held 51% of the equity and contained wording such as "the shareholders' resolution is as follows," without any content regarding loan guarantees, which fully demonstrated that Cheng Junping held equity in Niuxinda Company. 2. Niuxinda Company had previously acknowledged the sample materials for the appraisal. At the first-instance trial, it explicitly stated no objection to the appraisal conclusion, and the first-instance judgment's acceptance of the appraisal conclusion was correct. 3. The relevant gmail and 126 email accounts had been notarized, the emails were signed by Zhang Feng or Frank (Zhang Feng's other email name), and the content was all related to Niuxinda Company's business. The existing evidence was sufficient to prove that Cheng Junping was a shareholder of Niuxinda Company. Cheng Junping requested the dismissal of the appeal and affirmation of the original judgment.

The third party at first instance, Zhang Feng, stated that he agreed with the appellant Niuxinda Company's arguments.

The third party at first instance, Cheng Lan, stated that he agreed with the appellee Cheng Junping's arguments.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, upon second-instance trial, confirmed the facts found by the first-instance court.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held at second instance that:

Since the appellee Cheng Junping is a U.S. citizen, this case is a foreign-related dispute. Article 14 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations provides that "matters such as the civil capacity, civil conduct capacity, organizational structure, and shareholder rights and obligations of a legal person and its branches shall be governed by the law of the place of registration." As a dispute over shareholder qualification confirmation, the appellant Niuxinda Company's place of registration is within the territory of the People's Republic of China, so the law of the People's Republic of China shall apply to this case.

The issue at second instance was whether the third party at first instance, Zhang Feng, held on behalf of the appellee Cheng Junping 26% of the equity of the appellant Niuxinda Company.

First, from the language of the contracts, the Share Agreement dated November 10, 2009, stated that the appellee Cheng Junping, the third party at first instance Zhang Feng, and Cheng Lan would "initially establish a company in the names of Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan, and once conditions mature, Cheng Junping and this company would establish a Sino-foreign joint venture." Regarding the initially established company, the three agreed "to establish Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Co., Ltd. in the names of Zhang Feng and Cheng Lan," and the reason for this arrangement was that "Cheng Junping is a U.S. citizen and currently cannot establish a joint venture with a domestic natural person," while the actual investment ratio was "Cheng Junping 51%, Zhang Feng 25%, Cheng Lan 24%." The language of the agreement was clear and unambiguous, contradicting the claims of the appellant Niuxinda Company and Zhang Feng that the agreement meant a future joint venture between Niuxinda Company and Cheng Junping, rather than the establishment of Niuxinda Company itself. Subsequently, the Share Agreement dated October 29, 2012, further stated, "After consultation among Cheng Junping, Zhang Feng, and Cheng Lan, the shareholders' resolution is as follows: ... Based on the respective shareholding ratios in Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Company of the three persons, the actual ownership ratios of the three persons in Shanghai Yiyue Investment Management Co., Ltd. are as follows: Cheng Junping holds 51% of the company's equity, Zhang Feng holds 25% of the company's equity, and Cheng Lan holds 24% of the company's equity ..." Since "Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Company holds 100% equity of Shanghai Yiyue Investment Management Co., Ltd.," two conclusions can be drawn from the above agreement: First, all three persons at that time confirmed that Cheng Junping was a shareholder of Niuxinda Company; Second, Cheng Junping held 51% of the equity of Niuxinda Company. The Share Agreement did not contain any mention of the loan guarantee matter alleged by Niuxinda Company and Zhang Feng, and Niuxinda Company and Zhang Feng did not provide any other evidence regarding the loan guarantee. Their claim lacked factual basis.

Second, regarding the appraisal opinion of the Capital Contribution Certificate. At first instance, upon the application of the appellant Niuxinda Company, the appraisal institution issued an appraisal opinion. On December 30, 2019, during the cross-examination of the appraisal opinion, Niuxinda Company and the third party at first instance Zhang Feng stated, "no objection to the appraisal conclusion," while also arguing that "page 2 contains two sample materials dated August 6, but the Capital Contribution Certificate is also dated August 6 but cannot be confirmed, which corroborates that the authenticity of the Capital Contribution Certificate is uncertain." They held a similar view at second instance. The second-instance court held that the opinions of Niuxinda Company and Zhang Feng were merely their subjective judgments without factual basis and could not override the valid appraisal opinion. Considering the burden of proof and the appraisal opinion, it should be held that the objections raised by Niuxinda Company and Zhang Feng to the Capital Contribution Certificate were unfounded, and the Capital Contribution Certificate should be accepted. According to the Capital Contribution Certificate, the appellee Cheng Junping was a shareholder of Niuxinda Company and had paid a capital contribution of RMB 510,000 on November 3, 2009.

Third, regarding the attribution of the email accounts. Based on daily experience, registering and using email accounts typically does not require strict real-name authentication procedures, so it is difficult to directly determine the owner of the email accounts zhangfeng0117@gmail.com and zhangfeng_117@126.com by querying their registration information. However, this does not mean that the actual user of the email accounts cannot be inferred. The second-instance court held that the determination could be made from the following two aspects: First, from the form, the core field of the above email account names is "zhangfeng," which matches the pinyin letters of the third party at first instance Zhang Feng, and the sender of these emails is also named "Zhang Feng," which is the same name as Zhang Feng. Second, from the content, the emails exchanged between these accounts and the appellee Cheng Junping and others involved monthly account details, financial statements, factory location selection, foreign exchange settlement schedules, and other information. Such detailed internal information would be difficult to obtain without being responsible for the daily operations of the appellant Niuxinda Company, and the legal representative of Niuxinda Company is Zhang Feng. Considering all these factors, the first-instance court's finding that the above email accounts were actually used by Zhang Feng was not improper.

In summary, the second-instance court found that the appellee Cheng Junping was a shareholder of the appellant Niuxinda Company, and the 26% equity of Niuxinda Company held in the name of the third party at first instance Zhang Feng should belong to Cheng Junping. The second-instance court also noted that the Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China abolished the restriction in the original Sino-foreign equity joint venture law that a Chinese natural person could not be a joint venture partner. Furthermore, Article 3 of the Implementing Regulations of the Foreign Investment Law of the People's Republic of China clarifies that "other investors referred to in Article 2, paragraph 2, items 1 and 3 of the Foreign Investment Law include Chinese natural persons." Given that China implements a pre-establishment national treatment plus negative list management system for foreign investment, the first-instance court also sent a letter to the relevant administrative authority during the first-instance proceedings and received a reply stating, "... The business of Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Co., Ltd. does not fall within the scope of the Special Administrative Measures (Negative List) for Foreign Investment Access, ... There are no legal obstacles to my commission handling the change of Carson Jun Ping Cheng to a shareholder of Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Co., Ltd. and the filing procedures for changing Shanghai Niuxinda Import & Export Co., Ltd. to a foreign-invested enterprise." Therefore, Cheng Junping's request to be registered as a shareholder of Niuxinda Company does not require special approval procedures and faces no legal or policy obstacles.

In conclusion, the first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and the judgment was correct. The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 24 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China (III), subparagraph 1 of Article 170 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 334 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on May 14, 2020:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed.
